title: 17 — Design Nearby Friends
html:
17 — Design Nearby Friends

The one idea: unlike businesses (chapter 16), friends move, so the problem is a firehose of location updates that are only interesting for a few minutes. Keep the latest location in a TTL cache, and route updates to friends through Redis pub/sub channels — one per user — over persistent WebSocket connections. The database only stores history, off the hot path.

Step 1 — Scope

  • Users who opt in see friends within 5 miles, with distance and last-updated time.
  • List refreshes every few seconds; locations updated every 30 s.
  • Inactive friends (> 10 min) disappear.
  • 1 billion users, 10% use the feature → 100M DAU; 10M concurrent users; avg 400 friends.
  • Store location history for ML/analytics.

Estimates: 10M concurrent ÷ 30 s ≈ 334,000 location updates/s.

Step 2 — High-level design

In theory peer-to-peer; in practice a shared backend that fans out each update to the user's active friends.

---
title: Nearby friends — high-level architecture
---
flowchart LR
    M["Mobile client"] <-->|WebSocket| WS["WebSocket servers<br/>(stateful)"]
    M -->|HTTP| API["API servers<br/>(profile, friends, auth)"]
    WS --> LC[("Location cache<br/>Redis, TTL")]
    WS --> PS["Redis pub/sub<br/>(channel per user)"]
    PS --> WS
    WS --> LH[("Location history DB<br/>Cassandra-style")]
    API --> UDB[("User DB")]

Update flow

  1. Client sends (lat, lng, ts) over its WebSocket.
  2. WebSocket server writes it to location history (async) and to the location cache (TTL ≈ 10 min, refreshed on each update).
  3. Publishes to the user's pub/sub channel.
  4. Every online friend's WebSocket handler is subscribed to that channel → receives the update → computes distance → if within radius, pushes to the friend's client.

Initial load

On connect: fetch friends, batch-read their locations from the cache, compute distances, subscribe to each friend's channel.

Step 3 — Deep dive

3.1 Scaling each component

Component How it scales
API servers Stateless, autoscale
WebSocket servers Stateful → drain on scale-down (mark as draining, stop new connections, wait)
Location cache Only latest location per user; shard by user ID; memory ~ 10M × ~100 B = small; QPS is the concern → shard across Redis nodes
Redis pub/sub Channels are cheap (a hash table entry + subscriber list). Bottleneck is CPU for message fan-out: 334k updates × ~100 active friends each ≈ ~14M pushes/s → a cluster of ~100+ pub/sub servers, sharded by channel with consistent hashing
Location history Write-heavy → Cassandra-style wide-column store, sharded by user ID

3.2 Scaling pub/sub servers

  • Service discovery (etcd/ZooKeeper) holds the hash ring of pub/sub servers; WebSocket servers cache it.
  • Pub/sub cluster is stateful (subscriber lists) → treat resizing like a stateful DB migration: over-provision, resize during low traffic, and expect a burst of resubscriptions.

3.3 Adding/removing friends

On friend add/remove, the client's WebSocket handler subscribes/unsubscribes to that friend's channel.

3.4 Users with many friends

Hard cap on friends (e.g. 5,000) keeps fan-out bounded. The load for a well-connected user spreads across many pub/sub servers anyway.

3.5 Nearby random people (opt-in)

Add one channel per geohash cell: users subscribe to their cell (and neighbours) and publish updates to it. Same machinery, different channel keys.

3.6 Alternative to Redis pub/sub

An actor/ Erlang-style system (one lightweight process per user; message passing between processes) fits this problem naturally — it's what large chat/presence systems use.

Step 4 — Wrap-up

Key points: WebSocket for bidirectional low latency, Redis for ephemeral location with TTL, pub/sub for fan-out, stateful tier draining, and history written asynchronously. Privacy: locations are sensitive — encrypt, minimise retention, respect opt-out instantly.

.NET / Azure mapping

  • Azure SignalR Service / Web PubSub for millions of concurrent connections; groups per user (group:friends-of:{userId}) replace raw pub/sub channels.
  • Azure Cache for Redis (clustered): latest location with SET loc:{user} … EX 600; Redis pub/sub or Streams for fan-out; GEOADD/GEOSEARCH for the "nearby strangers" variant.
  • Microsoft Orleans — the .NET actor model: one grain per user holding its latest location and online friends; grains message each other directly. Arguably the most natural .NET design for this problem.
  • History: Event Hubs → Data Lake / Azure Data Explorer for analytics (write-heavy, time-series).

Review checklist

  • Update rate estimate (hundreds of thousands/s).
  • Why the DB is not on the hot path; TTL cache instead.
  • Pub/sub channel per user; fan-out math.
  • Stateful WebSocket and pub/sub tiers — draining and resizing.
  • Friend add/remove updates subscriptions.
  • Privacy.
